{"id": "98:1/q20", "question": "What prior expectation or demand for proof is reported?", "turns_on": "Whether it came from scriptural promise, pagan oath, or coordinated challenge.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q20/p1", "position": "Scripturalists expected a prophet or book and invoked him against opponents, then rejected him.", "reasons": "Muqātil reports their question; Biqāʿī describes their hope of victory. Ibn ʿĀshūr quotes Deuteronomy and Gospel promises, including lasting law and worldwide testimony."}, {"id": "98:1/q20/p2", "position": "Polytheists promised to be better guided if given a warning scripture yet later demanded further signs.", "reasons": "Muqātil cites 37:168–169; Biqāʿī cites 35:42; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 6:156–157, 28:48 and 21:5."}, {"id": "98:1/q20/p3", "position": "Jewish opponents supplied Quraysh with objections and tests as Islam spread.", "reasons": "Islāḥī says they first hoped Quraysh would suppress Islam, then suggested the sacrificial-fire test; Burṣawī says scripturalists altered Muhammad's descriptions."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q21", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from the opening?", "turns_on": "Which veil or inner attachment is described.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q21/p1", "position": "Scripturalists are veiled from the path to the Real; polytheists from the Real itself.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says both persist until proof, compares sects awaiting the Mahdī, and fears similarly frustrated expectations."}, {"id": "98:1/q21/p2", "position": "The sūra distinguishes people freed from desire from people captive to it.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī links reverent fear, avoidance of doubt and leaving what displeases God to 35:28."}, {"id": "98:1/q21/p3", "position": "The basmala can be an avenue of forgiveness, aid, insight and nearness.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī distinguishes sinners, obedient, learned and gnostics."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q22", "question": "Where and when was the sūra revealed?", "turns_on": "Whether the setting is Mecca or Medina.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q22/p1", "position": "It was revealed in Medina.", "reasons": "Māwardī, Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀshūr favor Medina; Ubayy's Medinan report, disputes with scripturalists and declarative style are cited. Ibn ʿĀshūr dates it around late year three or early year four, after al-Ṭalāq and before al-Ḥashr."}, {"id": "98:1/q22/p2", "position": "It was revealed in Mecca.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it better known; reports name ʿĀʾisha and Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās. Qutb says scripturalists and zakāh could occur in a Meccan sūra."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q23", "question": "How many verses are counted in the sūra?", "turns_on": "Whether the count is seven, eight, or nine.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q23/p1", "position": "Most count eight.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts nine in Basra; Jishumī reports eight outside Basra."}, {"id": "98:1/q23/p2", "position": "Basra counts nine.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports nine; Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr contrast eight elsewhere."}, {"id": "98:1/q23/p3", "position": "Basra counts seven.", "reasons": "Jishumī alone records seven for Basra."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q24", "question": "What titles are recorded for the sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q24/p1", "position": "Lam Yakun, al-Bayyina, al-Qayyima, Ahl al-Kitāb, al-Bariyya and al-Infikāk occur, with further variants.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr counts six, tracing Lam Yakun to the Prophet's speech to Ubayy; Ālūsī also lists al-Qiyāma, al-Balad and al-Munfakkīn."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q25", "question": "What merit is reported for reciting the sūra?", "turns_on": "Which promised reward, and how the report is rated.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q25/p1", "position": "God hears recitation and grants Paradise until satisfied, never forgetting the reciter.", "reasons": "Variants name Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Ḥakīm and Maṭar or Naẓīr al-Muzanī or al-Madanī; Ibn Kathīr calls one route extremely rare."}, {"id": "98:1/q25/p2", "position": "A reciter will be with the best of creation on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "This is transmitted as a Prophetic promise."}, {"id": "98:1/q25/p3", "position": "People would give up family and wealth to learn it, and angels protect reciters.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī calls the report unsound and Ibn al-ʿArabī calls its version false."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q26", "question": "What happened when the Prophet recited it to Ubayy?", "turns_on": "Whether the command concerned this sūra or the Qurʾān and how Ubayy responded.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q26/p1", "position": "God ordered the Prophet to recite the sūra to Ubayy; Ubayy heard he was named and wept.", "reasons": "The sound Anas version is in Bukhārī and Muslim. Other routes name Abū Ḥayya, Abū Ḥubba or Abū Khaythama; one says Ubayy rejoiced and cited 10:58."}, {"id": "98:1/q26/p2", "position": "The command was to recite Qurʾān to Ubayy, including this sūra.", "reasons": "Qatāda's variant says Qurʾān broadly; Ibn Kathīr calls an unusual al-Ṭabarānī route strange and prefers the established reports."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q27", "question": "Why did the Prophet recite it to Ubayy?", "turns_on": "Whether for teaching, humility, transmission, or reassurance.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q27/p1", "position": "It reassured and strengthened Ubayy after a reading dispute and doubt.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr compares recitation of al-Fatḥ to ʿUmar after Ḥudaybiyya, citing 48:27; Biqāʿī relates the al-Naḥl dispute and Ubayy's relief."}, {"id": "98:1/q27/p2", "position": "It taught humility despite differences in rank.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports this explanation; Biqāʿī warns against learned status obstructing acceptance."}, {"id": "98:1/q27/p3", "position": "A teacher may recite to a learner.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī draws this legal lesson."}, {"id": "98:1/q27/p4", "position": "Ubayy's quick understanding enabled exact transmission and teaching others.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports the explanation."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q28", "question": "What extra material accompanied Ubayy's recitation, and was it Qurʾān?", "turns_on": "Whether the wealth and hanīf sayings were revealed text or Prophetic speech.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q28/p1", "position": "Reports add sayings on Adam's unending desire for wealth, repentance, hanīf monotheism, deeds and reward.", "reasons": "The versions differ; Ibn ʿAbbās reports ʿUmar asking whether to write the two-valleys saying, while Ubayy remained unsure if it was revelation or Prophetic speech."}, {"id": "98:1/q28/p2", "position": "The added two-valleys saying is not part of the Qurʾānic recitation.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr al-Anbārī cites connected readings through Ubayy omitting it, its known Prophetic wording and consensus."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q29", "question": "What seven-aḥruf report accompanies Ubayy's story?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q29/p1", "position": "Gabriel successively permitted one, two, three then seven aḥruf, each sufficient and correct.", "reasons": "The Prophet sought ease for his community. Abū Dāwūd's wording permits synonymous attributes but forbids ending a punishment verse with mercy or vice versa."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q30", "question": "Does accountability wait for a messenger's proof?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q30/p1", "position": "Punishment or condemnation waits until a messenger or decisive proof clarifies obligations.", "reasons": "Elmalılı cites 17:15 and calls the interval excusable; Asad cites 6:131–132, 17:15 and 42:13; Study Quran says it may concern Muhammad's prophethood rather than God's existence."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q31", "question": "What do the purified pages and upright religion contain?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis falls on scriptural purity, monotheism, rites, or righteous works.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q31/p1", "position": "The commanded core is sincere worship of God, prayer and almsgiving.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī says qayyima can refer to community or law, or intensify the sense; another view makes it the books' injunction, comparing 2:213."}, {"id": "98:1/q31/p2", "position": "The Messenger recites books purified of falsehood containing upright, just divine rulings.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī explains the next verses' ṣuḥuf and kutub this way."}, {"id": "98:1/q31/p3", "position": "Ḥunafāʾ can denote pilgrimage or Abrahamic rites including circumcision and marriage limits.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as pilgrims; Qatāda and Saʿīd ibn Ḥamza add circumcision, ritual observance and prohibited close-relative marriage."}, {"id": "98:1/q31/p4", "position": "Qayyima can be the plural of qayyim or qāʾim, describing upholders of monotheism.", "reasons": "Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl reports al-Khalīl's analysis."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q32", "question": "How is al-bariyya read in the later judgment verse?", "turns_on": "Whether it is pronounced with hamza.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q32/p1", "position": "Nāfiʿ and Ibn Dhakwān read hamzated al-bariʾa.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī calls this the original form."}, {"id": "98:1/q32/p2", "position": "Others omit the hamza and double the consonant.", "reasons": "One account says a resembling consonant replaces the removed hamza."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q01", "question": "What does rasūl mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q01/p1", "position": "An emissary sent by God.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī glosses it as one sent by God."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q02", "question": "Who is the messenger in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse identifies the historical Prophet, Gabriel or the angel demanded by opponents, or speaks generally of messengers.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q02/p1", "position": "Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Māwardī, al-Nasafī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and others identify him. Al-Ālūsī prefers Muhammad as transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil and objects that the angelic interpretation makes the pages into revelation weakly. Ibn ʿĀshūr says earlier scriptures expected a law-bearing messenger like Moses or Jesus; al-Ghazālī points to his miraculous ch

aracter and many miracles."}, {"id": "98:2/q02/p2", "position": "Gabriel, reciting angelic copies of the Preserved Tablet.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī reports Gabriel; al-Ālūsī reports and rejects an elaboration with angelic copies, calling the resulting sense of pages as revelation weak."}, {"id": "98:2/q02/p3", "position": "An angel directly sent by God to read written pages, as the opponents demanded.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the opponents demanded an angel and written messages read aloud, rather than a human claiming revelation."}, {"id": "98:2/q02/p4", "position": "The messengers sent to every community.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 35:24, that every community had a warner, and extends the phrase to messengers and their revelations generally."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q03", "question": "How is rasūl constructed after al-bayyina?", "turns_on": "Whether the indefinite nominative continues the definite bayyina through apposition or begins a new sentence; some analyses supply an omitted noun.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q03/p1", "position": "It is nominative apposition explaining the clear proof, directly or through an understood noun.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and the majority make it appositional. Al-Samīn allows inclusion or emphatic whole-for-whole apposition; an omitted noun can mean the Messenger's proof. Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī allow an understood proof, revelation, miracle or book when bayyina is the Qur'an. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this compressed appositional style and says it presents the expected proof as already arrived."}, {"id": "98:2/q03/p2", "position": "It starts an explanatory nominal sentence with an omitted subject: it or he is a messenger.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ treats the indefinite noun as a fresh nominative after the definite proof; al-Ṭabarī compares 85:15–16. Al-Akhfash supplies 'it is.' Ibn ʿĀshūr allows a stop after 'until the proof comes,' then a parenthetic explanation before 98:4. Al-Ālūsī also allows rasūl as predicate of an omitted subject."}, {"id": "98:2/q03/p3", "position": "It is an independent subject, with yatlū as its predicate, or a sentence inserted to explain or praise the proof.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports these further analyses, including a modifier of bayyina when that word means Qur'an."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q04", "question": "How is rasūl read and parsed in the reported variants?", "turns_on": "The nominative common text versus the accusative attributed to Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd, with competing parses of the accusative.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q04/p1", "position": "The common reading is nominative rasūlun.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān attribute the nominative to the majority; it is commonly parsed as apposition to bayyina."}, {"id": "98:2/q04/p2", "position": "Ubayy and/or Ibn Masʿūd read accusative rasūlan, parsed as a circumstantial, detached or specification accusative.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ names Ubayy; al-Jishumī names Ibn Masʿūd; al-Qurṭubī and others report both. Al-Samīn says the circumstantial parse retains the same hyperbole or ellipsis as the nominative analysis."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q05", "question": "What does min Allāh modify?", "turns_on": "Whether the prepositional phrase qualifies the messenger or the scrolls.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q05/p1", "position": "It modifies rasūl, describing the messenger as sent from God.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Bursawī take it as a modifier; al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say it is adjectival rather than a genitive construction."}, {"id": "98:2/q05/p2", "position": "It can be circumstantial to the scrolls, meaning they descended from God.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ allows this alternative as transmitted by al-Samīn."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q06", "question": "Why say 'a messenger from God' in this form?", "turns_on": "Whether the form signals eminence, the kind of awaited proof, or an ellipsis in the source phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q06/p1", "position": "The indefinite noun magnifies the messenger, and 'from God' adds honor and grandeur.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī describes an exceptionally eminent messenger; al-Ālūsī says the indefinite and divine source reinforce each other. Ibn ʿĀshūr says avoiding iḍāfa permits the magnifying tanwīn. Al-Bursawī calls the source an honor."}, {"id": "98:2/q06/p2", "position": "The indefinite presents a type of awaited messenger, making the proof easier to recognize.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 'numbered days' in 2:184 and the transition to 'a Book' in 7:1–2."}, {"id": "98:2/q06/p3", "position": "The wording can omit an understood ʿind, 'from the presence of God'.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī's Burhān compares 2:147, 19:45 and 5:15, with 'from God' making the ellipsis apparent."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q07", "question": "What does yatlū mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is given its ordinary recitation sense or Qatāda's explanatory sense of fine remembrance and praise.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q07/p1", "position": "To recite or read aloud.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Qurṭubī give the basic gloss; Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies repeating speech without addition or omission, from writing or memory, so the verb indicates the revealed wording is unchanged. Al-Biqāʿī calls the recitation mass-transmitted and taught by God."}, {"id": "98:2/q07/p2", "position": "To present and praise the Qur'an in the finest terms.", "reasons": "Qatāda's recurrent gloss treats the messenger's tilāwa as excellent recollection and praise of the Qur'an; Ibn Abī Ḥātim adds that the purified pages are the Qur'an."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q08", "question": "How does the yatlū clause attach grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether rasūl already has a predicate and yatlū qualifies it, supplies a circumstance, or itself predicates the subject.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q08/p1", "position": "It is another adjective describing the messenger.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī, al-Ālūsī, al-Samīn and Ibn ʿĀshūr give this parse; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it also inserts praise of the Qur'an, a description not apparently in earlier promises."}, {"id": "98:2/q08/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause attached to the pronoun in the preceding modifier.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn conditions this on min Allāh being an adjective of rasūl; al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr also allow it."}, {"id": "98:2/q08/p3", "position": "It can be the predicate of rasūl.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī allows this when rasūl is treated as a nominal subject; al-Ālūsī reports the same analysis."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q09", "question": "How can an unlettered messenger recite pages?", "turns_on": "Whether 'pages' is metonymy for the text memorized by Muhammad or points figuratively to earlier sheets confirmed by his recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q09/p1", "position": "He recites the pages' written contents from memory; 'pages' stands for their contents.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī and Ibn ʿĀshūr invoke his unlettered state. Al-Ālūsī calls it metonymy and reports an omitted 'like pages' or a reader metaphor; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 29:48. Al-Rāzī adds a book attributed to Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq suggesting he could read, but not write, perhaps miraculously."}, {"id": "98:2/q09/p2", "position": "He recites the Qur'an that confirms the earlier sheets' fundamental laws, so its recited content is treated as those sheets.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī calls the attribution figurative because the Qur'an confirms earlier sheets in the foundations of laws and rulings."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q10", "question": "What does ṣuḥuf mean literally?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q10/p1", "position": "Sheets, pages or surfaces that hold writing; the plural of ṣaḥīfa.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī give the plural and material sense; al-Ālūsī relates it to spreading out. Ibn ʿĀshūr lists parchment, leather and cloth. ʿAyn al-Maʿānī says sheets are laid one over another; Iṣlāḥī stresses that the demanded message had to be written and read aloud."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q11", "question": "Which pages does the messenger recite?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣuḥuf points to the recited Qur'an, its heavenly source, angelic copies, earlier scripture, or an inward celestial reality.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q11/p1", "position": "The Qur'an, its written contents or revealed portions.", "reasons": "Muqātil says any writing may be called pages and the Qur'an has many kinds of qualities. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatāda specify its written sheets. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls them revealed portions, citing 80:13–16; al-Kāshifī says the term honors the Qur'an, which gathers all scriptures' secrets."}, {"id": "98:2/q11/p2", "position": "Heavenly pages or the Mother of the Book, from which revealed books descend.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan places them in heaven; al-Ṭabrisī adds that purified angels alone touch them. Al-Qurṭubī relates them to the heavenly original and 85:21–22; Ibn Kathīr connects purified heavenly sheets to 80:13–16. Study Quran names the Preserved Tablet and 85:22 and 97:1–2."}, {"id": "98:2/q11/p3", "position": "Angelic copies from the Preserved Tablet recited by Gabriel.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this alternative but rejects its treatment of the pages as revelation as weak."}, {"id": "98:2/q11/p4", "position": "Tablets of celestial intellects and souls.", "reasons": "In al-Qāshānī's inward reading they are reached by detachment from natural, material and human corruption and contain enduring just foundations of true religion."}, {"id": "98:2/q11/p5", "position": "Earlier prophetic scriptures, whose foundations the Qur'an confirms.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī offers a connection between Muhammad's mission and scriptures sent to earlier prophets; al-Bursawī says Qur'anic recitation figuratively counts as reciting those earlier sheets because it confirms their laws."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q12", "question": "Why is the revelation called pages?", "turns_on": "Whether the designation depends on current contents, future writing, honor, or the physical form of sheets.", "p

ositions": [{"id": "98:2/q12/p1", "position": "The written surface names its contents by close association.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the physical sheets stand for their contents; al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr make the same metonymic point, Ibn ʿĀshūr citing 29:48."}, {"id": "98:2/q12/p2", "position": "The revelation is called pages in anticipation of its being written.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says God ordered it written, compares Joseph's 'pressing wine' in 12:36, and names sheets, sheep shoulder blades, scraps and stones; 29:51 supports calling the recited revelation a Book."}, {"id": "98:2/q12/p3", "position": "The term honors the Qur'an as containing the secrets of all scriptures.", "reasons": "Al-Kāshifī gives this explanation through al-Bursawī; Muqātil adds that it contains many kinds of qualities."}, {"id": "98:2/q12/p4", "position": "Sheets are named for being laid one upon another.", "reasons": "ʿAyn al-Maʿānī, as quoted by al-Bursawī, explains the name by their physical arrangement."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q13", "question": "In what sense are the pages purified?", "turns_on": "Purity is explained by the text's truth, its praised status, restrictions on touching, divine origin, or an inward celestial state.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q13/p1", "position": "They and their contents are free of falsehood, unbelief, shirk, error, distortion and misleading material.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās lists lies, doubt, hypocrisy and error; Muqātil and ʿIkrima add shirk; al-Zajjāj cites 41:42 and 80:14. Al-Qurṭubī treats the varying lists as one sense. Al-Qushayrī stresses protection from disbelievers' alteration; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī from devils' intrusion. Ibn ʿĀshūr sees clear, unambiguous meaning and an allusion to corruption in some earlier scriptures."}, {"id": "98:2/q13/p2", "position": "They are honored with the finest praise and commended judgments.", "reasons": "Qatāda's gloss ties purity to excellent remembrance and judgment; al-Rāzī says the Qur'an is free of blameworthy mention and receives the best praise."}, {"id": "98:2/q13/p3", "position": "Only purified people or angels may touch them.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Biqāʿī cite or echo 56:79; al-Ṭabrisī places the pages in heaven with purified angels. Iṣlāḥī says no human or jinn has touched them, only God and angels. Al-Bursawī and Elmalılı combine this with freedom from falsehood."}, {"id": "98:2/q13/p4", "position": "Their origin from God makes them pure.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives divine descent as a further possibility."}, {"id": "98:2/q13/p5", "position": "They are free of material and human corruption through spiritual detachment.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī applies purity to tablets of celestial intellects and souls."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q14", "question": "What exactly does the adjective 'purified' describe?", "turns_on": "Whether the adjective is transferred to sheets from their textual contents or from those who may touch them.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q14/p1", "position": "It grammatically describes the sheets but in meaning describes the Qur'an contained in them.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī explicitly distinguish grammar from intended content; al-Qurṭubī compares the honored purified sheets of 80:13–14. Al-Ālūsī calls freedom from falsehood a metaphor or transferred description."}, {"id": "98:2/q14/p2", "position": "It describes the pages themselves as ritually accessible only to the purified.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī allows a figurative transfer to the pages from the people permitted to touch them; al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī relate this to 56:79."}]}
{"id": "98:2/q15", "question": "What is the clear proof identified by this description?", "turns_on": "Whether bayyina denotes the Messenger, the Qur'an, both together, or the evident disclosure of truth.", "positions": [{"id": "98:2/q15/p1", "position": "Muhammad, the messenger whose person and signs clarify truth.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Māwardī, al-Baghawī and others identify the proof with the Messenger. Al-Wāḥidī calls bayyina manifest evidence and allows a prophet or just witness; Muqātil says he exposed error and shirk. {"id": "98:3/q21", "question": "How can readers recognize Qur'anic inimitability?", "turns_on": "The reader's command of Arabic eloquence and differences of expert taste.", "positions": [{"id": "98:3/q21/p1", "position": "Non-Arabs infer it from the Arabs' failed challenge.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī says one unable to master Arabic is still less able to match the Qur'an."}, {"id": "98:3/q21/p2", "position": "Arabic speakers lacking mastery of style rely on the same indirect evidence.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī distinguishes language knowledge from mastery of eloquence and forms."}, {"id": "98:3/q21/p3", "position": "Masters of Arabic style directly perceive speech beyond human limits.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī likens them to money changers and cloth merchants discerning qualities others miss; expert tastes can still differ."}, {"id": "98:3/q21/p4", "position": "Experts differ in taste for weighty, flowing, or obscure speech.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports preferences for solidity, graceful clarity, and rare diction."}]}
{"id": "98:3/q22", "question": "What poetic example is cited for judging speech and people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "98:3/q22/p1", "position": "ʿUmar praised Zuhayr for praising people only for traits they possessed.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports that ʿUmar then addressed ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥaṣḥāṣ after a line about age and Islam restraining a man."}]}
{"id": "98:3/q23", "question": "How was Majaz al-Qur'an used and assessed by later scholars?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "98:3/q23/p1", "position": "It remained an influential reference despite criticism, used by many later scholars.", "reasons": "The writer notes a missing Cairo section criticizing Abū ʿUbayda, making its value hard to assess; al-Ṭabarī's objections appear in footnotes. Users named include Ibn Qutayba, al-Bukhārī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Yazīdī, al-Zajjāj, Ibn Durayd, al-Sijistānī, Ibn al-Naḥḥās, al-Azharī, Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, al-Jawharī, Abū ʿUbayd al-Harawī, Ibn Barrī and Ibn Ḥajar; a detailed study of al-Bukhārī's use is deferred."}]}
{"id": "105:5/q01", "question": "What does the initial fa indicate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "105:5/q01/p1", "position": "It marks the swift, immediate result of the birds' stone throwing.", "reasons": "Elmalılı calls it both causal and sequential."}]}
{"id": "105:5/q02", "question": "How is fa-jaʿalahum read, and who is its agent?", "turns_on": "The reported verb forms and whether God or the birds are grammatical subject.", "positions": [{"id": "105:5/q02/p1", "position": "He made them: God is the agent of the destruction.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī says the alternative 'left them' can carry this same result. Biqāʿī says the devastation was God's creative act, beyond the stones' ordinary effect."}, {"id": "105:5/q02/p2", "position": "He left them like eaten chaff.", "reasons": "Abū al-Malīḥ or Abū al-Khalīj al-Hudhalī is named for fatarakahum; Ibn Jinnī says this stresses their remaining in the ruined state."}, {"id": "105:5/q02/p3", "position": "The birds made them like eaten chaff.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports fajaʿalat-hum, with still tāʾ and fatḥa on lām, taking the feminine birds as subject."}]}
{"id": "105:5/q03", "question": "How does the kāf of comparison work?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "105:5/q03/p1", "position": "It introduces the comparison, even alongside an expressed 'like' or mithl.", "reasons": "Sībawayh cites Hamīd al-Arqaṭ's rajaz for kāf after mithl. Al-Qurṭubī parallels 42:11, where kāf accompanies mithl. Al-Naḥḥās calls the kāf phrase the second object of jaʿala."}]}
{"id": "105:5/q04", "question": "What is ʿaṣf?", "turns_on": "Which part or stage of the crop the word names: green foliage, straw, grain husk, tender tips, emptied grain, or edible plant matter.", "positions": [{"id": "105:5/q04/p1", "position": "Crop foliage, especially wheat leaves, including leaves left after harvest.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd, Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Hishām identify leaves; Ibn Hishām says uncut leaves. Al-ʿAlqama's verse supports ʿuṣayfa as foliage. Elmalılı calls green foliage the basic sense, later drying into straw, and translates it Turkish hasıl; al-Ḥasan remembers barley shoots called ʿaṣīf in Medina. Al-Majāz also gives ʿaṣīfa; al-Qurṭubī lists singulars ʿaṣfa, ʿaṣāfa, ʿaṣīfa. Al-ʿAṣf can be crop or vegetable foliage."}, {"id": "105:5/q04/p2", "position": "Straw or chaff, the dry crop residue.", "reasons": "Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd, al-Ḥasan and Abū Muslim give straw; Saʿīd says common people call it habūr, while al-Ḍaḥḥāk reports Nabataean habūr, alternatively maqhur or maqūr. Abū Muslim cites 55:12 and winnowing wind separating straw from grain. Al-Muʾarrikh specifies broken stalks with fallen tips. Elmalılı derives the noun or verbal noun from bending, twisting, breaking and scattering."}, {"id": "105:5/q04/p3", "position": "The outer husk covering a wheat grain.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās calls it the covering over the wheat; after the kernel is eaten or removed the husk remains. Al-Naḥḥās gives this also as a sense of maʾkūl. Ibn Jawzī and al-Rāzī refer the reader to 55:12 for ʿaṣf."}, {"id": "105:5/q04/p4", "position": "The tender tips of a crop before ears form.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ describes the pre-ripening tips; Elmalılı includes fresh pre-ear leaves in the reported range."}, {"id": "105:5/q04/p5", "position": "Grain or plant material made hollow when eaten.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima describes eaten grain as emptied; reports vary between grain and the plant."}, {"id": "105:5/q04/p6", "position": "Food or fodder.", "reasons": "Ḥabīb and Ḥusayn b. Thābit gloss the phrase as food; the Saʿīd and al-Ḥasan report calls the eaten material fresh fodder, qasīl. One Mawardī-Full note instead says the straw means figs."}]}
{"id": "105:5/q05", "question": "What state does 'eaten chaff' compare the army to?", "turns_on": "Whether the eating is by livestock, insects, or of the grain; whether maʾkūl names a completed act or what is edible.", "positions": [{"id": "105:5/q05/p1", "position": "Fodder eaten, digested and excreted by animals, then dried and scattered like the army's limbs.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī and others expressly compare dispersed dung to torn bodies. Ibn Zayd identifies crop and vegetable leaves passing through livestock. Al-Ālūsī says al-Kinānī's excrement provoking Abraha makes this resemblance apt. Elmalılı reports Ibn Jarīr and Fakhr al-Rāzī prefer this first reading; the source's summaries allow crushed or trampled fodder as its immediate stage."}, {"id": "105:5/q05/p2", "position": "Foliage gnawed or perforated by worms or insects, like the soldiers' pierced bodies.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj specifies rot or worms; Ṭāwūs says wheat leaves riddled with holes. Al-Biqāʿī connects holes to hot stones piercing head to anus and leaving black tunnels. Elmalılı says al-Zamakhsharī appears to favor this finer lexical image."}, {"id": "105:5/q05/p3", "position": "A crop whose grain has been eaten, leaving its husk or stalk hollow.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says the grain is understood as eaten; al-Qurṭubī likens it to calling a person handsome for his face. Al-Ālūsī allows ellipsis of a governing noun or figurative attribution; Elmalılı likewise says ellipsis or figurative attribution can evoke hollow bodies or burned insides. Ibn ʿAbbās says the grain is eaten and its husk blown away."}, {"id": "105:5/q05/p4", "position": "Fodder fit to be eaten, exposed and discarded for animals.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read maʾkūl as edible; Ibn Qutayba compares naming drinkable water. Al-Ālūsī's version leaves the dead abandoned in the desert, uncollected and unburied."}, {"id": "105:5/q05/p5", "position": "Chewed or trampled crop fragments show complete defeat, humiliation and bodily disintegration.", "reasons": "Al-Daḥḥāk and Ḥabīb speak of eaten crop or food; Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds baseness and vanishing clay. Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts lush foliage with fallen dead remains; Study Quran contrasts Arabia's great army with insignificant leaf remains. Qutb says insect chewing or animal grinding produces crumbs. Abū Muslim says eaten straw is spent, powerless and without return."}, {"id": "105:5/q05/p6", "position": "A mountain eaten hollow.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī transmits this unusual comparison from ʿIkrima."}]}
{"id": "105:5/q06", "question": "Why call the remains 'eaten' instead of naming their bodily end?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression alludes to the eventual excrement or is a tense device.", "positions": [{"id": "105:5/q06/p1", "position": "It decorously alludes to excreted, scattered refuse.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Biqāʿī, Elmalılı and others compare Qur'an 5:75, where Jesus and Mary are said to eat food. Bursevī compares 21:8. Al-Ālūsī says the blunt term would be indecorous; al-Burhān says eaten leaves eventually become dung. Islahi says the enemy is named by its eventual fate."}, {"id": "105:5/q06/p2", "position": "It casts a past consumption as present by replacing 'animals ate it'.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls this explanation strained."}]}
